rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four real newsroom doors, each with a different buyer, skeptic, payer, or business-model protagonist, and it keeps the proof burden in plain sight. Its strongest line, "The company that sells the app paid for the study that says the app works," is exactly the uncomfortable story a serious health reporter would chase. B has useful bones, especially "whether 'regular users' is doing the heavy lifting," but it poisons the well with an invented headline fact: "$70-a-year subscription." One bad made-up number in the subject line is how a pitch gets deleted and remembered.
gaps_in_A: "at a moment when demand for care exceeds clinician supply" is an invented backdrop; the update supplied no care-demand or clinician-supply fact.
"six times over" is a little overconfident because the update says "over 4 million" paid subscribers, so the exact ratio is not cleanly six.
The category and insurer angles are close cousins; A explains the distinction well, but both still depend on the same payer-benefit decision and could blur in a media list.
gaps_in_B: "$70-a-year subscription" is invented. The update says Calm has paid subscribers, not the annual price.
"once growth slows" is unsupported; no subscriber growth trend, churn, saturation, or slowdown data was supplied.
"Wellness apps are crossing from app-store impulse buy into reimbursed health benefit" asserts a plural trend from one Calm deal, then admits comparable examples are missing.
"AI-slop/sponsored-research skepticism journalists are writing about right now" is a fake external news peg; no current coverage or zeitgeist evidence was supplied.
